newsitem.title: GERMANY: Extended German shop hours get mixed response.
newsitem.headline: Extended German shop hours get mixed response.

text.p: Germans were at last allowed to shop late on Friday, after a law left over from the 1950s was loosened, but opponents said the change would damage family life and do little to boost sales.
Most Germans, who are keen window shoppers, seem to welcome the chance to shop outside normal work hours, thanks to a change in Europe's most restrictive retailing law.

The northern city of Bremen planned to celebrate the extension of shopping hours until 8 p.m. with musicians blowing trumpets and beating kettledrums. But sales clerks and owners of smaller shops said they dreaded the longer hours.

"I won't be able to spend as much time with my children and marriages will suffer. If men are left on their own while wives are at work, they are more likely to be unfaithful," said one saleswoman in Frankfurt's large Kaufhof department store.
Small retailers worry they will lose trade to the larger department stores, which initially lobbied for the change.

In other areas the new hours -- until 8 p.m. on weekdays and 4 p.m. on Saturdays -- were advertised only by small signs in store windows. The old weekday closing time was 6.30 p.m., with late closings on Thursday, and 2 p.m. on Saturdays.
The longer hours could ultimately release pent-up demand that has been diverted to spending on holidays or leisure.
"I think it's great. My till will be fuller and your purse will be emptier," said a sausage saleswoman in a major Frankfurt department store.

This Saturday, the new law will mean shops will close earlier than usual. The first Saturday of the month, known as "long Saturday," was previously a shopping frenzy, when shops stayed open until 6 p.m.. But doors will now close at 4 p.m. every week.
However, for three weeks a month shoppers will have two extra hours to spend their money on Saturdays.

Although politicians have said the longer hours will reduce unemployment, some shop workers say they will just work more inconvenient shifts for no extra money. Others will face longer days but will be compensated by additional holiday time.

"It is going to be a lot of very long days," said one sales clerk on Berlin's busy Kurfuerstendamm. "If you have to stand there under that artificial lighting all day long, you are bound to become exhausted."
Store unions, which led Germany's three million shop workers in warning strikes during the summer to win time off for extra late shifts, say staff will be spread more thinly.

"The thinner staffing will mean that service won't be better, but worse," said Margret Moenig-Raane of the HBV trade, banking and insurance union. Germany is not renowned for being a service-oriented culture.
Opponents of the law also question whether the longer hours will lead to an increase in turnover.

Some consumers and business people believe the law does not go far enough. "Frankfurt wants to be a world class city like London and New York," said French taxi-driver Danierl Diaz. "But everything is always closed. The hours still aren't long enough."
